# Introducing Synnax Desktop


The best of Synnax on a single bench, free for commercial use.


[Written by Emiliano Bonilla](https://www.linkedin.com/in/emiliano-bonilla-8a0a95187/)


A few weeks ago we launched Synnax Desktop. It’s the Synnax Core, Synnax Console, and Synnax Driver bundled together, built for the bench, and free for commercial use.


It’s also a big change in how we sell Synnax. For years, the only way to get your hands on it was to talk to us first. Desktop flips that around. In this post, I’ll walk you through what Desktop is, why we think it’s awesome, and why we decided to lead with the product instead of a sales process.


## Two ways to buy software


Nowadays, my job is mostly communication and sales. But before that, I was a laser focused systems engineer, and I spent a lot of time procuring software: databases, ETL tools, CI/CD pipelines, managed Kubernetes services, you name it.


It always went one of two ways.


Story 1 goes straight to sales. You submit a contact form, get on the phone with a sales rep, do a demo … or two … or three … and then spend weeks convincing your boss to pay for a product you’ve never actually used. And, often times, the really expensive tool you buy ends up not being what you expected.


There’s a common joke on industrial automation subreddits that goes like this:


From[r/PLC](https://redd.it/194jgm9)


Unlike the joke, the second pathway is different. Instead of submitting a form for a demo, you can download the product yourself. Sometimes the full-fledged version, sometimes with restricted use. You’re able to try it, enjoy using it, find value, and use practical deployment to show your team that the paid edition is a worthwhile investment.


If you’re an engineer, story 2 is dramatically better than story 1. You directly interact with the tool, see where it works and where it doesn’t, and decide if it’s worth your time and investment.


The companies and tools I respect the most operate this way: Linear, Vercel, and Figma. Most recently, I signed up for an enterprise subscription to[Paradev](https://paradev.com/) . The product was clearly so much better than anything else out there, that I knew I had to pay for it.


Desktop is our story 2. We’re putting the product first, and focusing deeply on the user experience and technical excellence. It’s a risk, but it’s one we’re happy to take because it’s the way we’d like to evaluate Synnax if we were engineers at our customers’ companies.


Here’s what trying out Desktop looks like.


That’s the whole sales process.


## So what is Synnax Desktop?


Synnax Desktop is a free edition of Synnax designed specifically for benchtop testing. It combines our Core, Console, and device drivers into what we think is one of the best desktop data acquisition, control, and data review tools on the market.


It’s easy to set up. Download and run Desktop, and it’ll immediately detect the data acquisition devices you have connected. The path from first seeing the tool to actually getting use out of it is as short as possible. Under the hood, we run the key components of the enterprise edition: device drivers, the Arc runtime, a Core, and the Console, all in one.


## What you can do with it


Once it’s open, you can:


1.


Connect your hardware


[NI devices](https://docs.synnaxlabs.com/reference/hardware/ni/configure-device) (on Windows),[LabJacks](https://docs.synnaxlabs.com/reference/hardware/labjack/configure-device) ,[Modbus](https://docs.synnaxlabs.com/reference/hardware/modbus/connect-server) and[OPC UA](https://docs.synnaxlabs.com/reference/hardware/opc-ua/connect-server) servers,[EtherCAT](https://docs.synnaxlabs.com/reference/hardware/ethercat/configure-device) I/O, and[HTTP](https://docs.synnaxlabs.com/reference/hardware/http/connect-server) APIs, all on the same bench at the same time.


2.


Watch it live, and go back to any run


Every sample is saved, so you can scroll back to[last Tuesday’s run](https://docs.synnaxlabs.com/reference/ranges) and[zoom](https://docs.synnaxlabs.com/reference/visualize/line-plots) from a week of data down to a single sample.


3.


Operate it from a schematic


[Draw your system](https://docs.synnaxlabs.com/reference/visualize/schematics) , drop in valves and gauges, and[click a valve to open it](https://docs.synnaxlabs.com/reference/control/manual) .


4.


Automate it with Arc


Write an[Arc](https://docs.synnaxlabs.com/blog/introducing-arc) sequence to fill the tank to 300 psi, hold for 10 seconds, vent, and abort if anything looks wrong.


5.


Script it from Python or TypeScript


Pull last week’s tests into a[notebook](https://docs.synnaxlabs.com/reference/client/read-data) , or[stream values](https://docs.synnaxlabs.com/reference/client/write-data) from your own script straight into a live plot.


No hardware on hand? Open the[sample project](https://docs.synnaxlabs.com/reference/get-started/sample-project) . It’s a simulated tank test that takes about five minutes.


## How does it compare?


You’ve probably got one of these on your bench already. Here’s the short version.


You build Control and sequences Price


**Synnax Desktop**


Nothing. Install it and go.


Schematics and Arc


Free, including commercial use


**LabVIEW**


The whole tool


Whatever you program


A quote from NI. Community is non-commercial.


**FlexLogger**


A logging configuration


Events in Pro, no sequencer


Lite is free. Professional is paid.


**InfluxDB + Grafana**


The integration and dashboards


None. That’s another script.


Free and open source


And here’s the long one.


### LabVIEW


LabVIEW is the most common by far. If you’re in a lab, there’s a good chance you’re either someone who uses a VI written by someone who left the company a while ago, or you’re in charge of maintaining bespoke VIs for different test applications. LabVIEW has clearly earned its place: decades of reliability improvements, integration with the NI hardware ecosystem, and awesome tooling like FPGA programming.


But good LabVIEW tools require good LabVIEW programmers. They are hard to come by, busy, and often times stretched thin in their work. If you want to do it yourself, you have to build the tool, and the free Community Edition is non-commercial. NI doesn’t list prices for the rest: you request a quote. Story 1 again.


Desktop is that tool, already built. If you need deterministic control on an FPGA, keep LabVIEW. For everything else on the bench, try Desktop.


### FlexLogger


FlexLogger is NI’s no-code data logger, and it’s the closest thing to Desktop out there. If your bench is all NI hardware, it’s a great way to get a logging setup running without writing a single line of LabVIEW. There’s a lot to like: it’s built by the same people who make the hardware, it’s easy to configure, and the Lite edition is free.


But FlexLogger is really built for NI hardware and for logging. Plenty of benches aren’t all NI, though. There’s a LabJack someone bought for a quick test, or a PLC talking Modbus, and connecting those means a plug-in built in LabVIEW. You can set up events in the Professional edition, but there’s no sequencer, so the moment you want to pressurize, hold, and vent, you’re back to writing LabVIEW or Python.


Desktop talks to all of that hardware at once, and runs your sequences in the same window you’re plotting in.


### InfluxDB and Grafana


InfluxDB and Grafana are what software engineers reach for. If someone on your team came from the software world, they’ve probably pitched it to you as the free option. And I get why: both are open source, Grafana makes beautiful dashboards, and for monitoring servers it’s hard to beat.


But neither tool was built for hardware. Nothing in the stack talks to a DAQ card, so someone has to write and maintain a script to get data in. Grafana can’t control anything, so opening a valve is another script. By default, dashboards also can’t refresh faster than every 5 seconds, which is fine for CPU usage but not for watching a pressure spike. By the time it all works, you’ve built a custom tool out of five different pieces, and someone has to own it.


Desktop is the whole stack in one tool, with no bolting together a DAQ, a Python script, Telegraf, InfluxDB, and Grafana. And the database underneath was built for sensor data: we[benchmarked it against InfluxDB and Timescale](https://docs.synnaxlabs.com/blog/one-billion-rows) .


## So why didn’t we do this sooner?


Honestly? Because story 1 works.


It lets you control the process. Instead of waiting for an engineer to fall in love with your tool, you can meticulously work through finding an engineering champion, running demos with the right stakeholders, and getting to procurement earlier.


It also works better for products that take a lot of work to fit into a customer’s infrastructure, and that was early Synnax. We often had to build significant new features before our tools worked with a customer’s hardware. If we’d handed out a free version as is, most people wouldn’t have found a fast enough path to value.


That’s no longer true. Synnax now works on a bench straight out of the box: plug in a LabJack, and you’re plotting data in minutes.


And deep down, all of us at Synnax are engineers. We want Synnax to be built by engineers, for engineers. Instead of being fed a problem and solution pair by a sales team, you should be able to discern for yourself where our product seriously unlocks productivity for your team, and where it doesn’t.


Synnax Desktop is a renewed, focused commitment to that ethos. We build tools for hardcore engineers, and we’re putting our product center stage as the evidence for how and why we build.


## When should you talk to us?


Remember the end of story 2? You show your team the paid edition is worth it, and then you start the sales process. Desktop is designed for every step before that one. And yes, it’s also designed to eventually make you interested in having a conversation with us about our enterprise edition.


Desktop is for one person on one computer, with up to 50 channels. Synnax Enterprise is for a team that shares one system. You run a Synnax Core on your own servers and get:


- Access from other computers, including the Console in a web browser.
- Users, roles, and permissions.
- Drivers on other computers, including NI CompactRIOs.
- Linux, Docker, and air-gapped deployments.
- As many channels as your license allows.


The day your bench turns into a test stand, or one engineer turns into five, is the day we’d love to talk.


For years, we asked engineers to take our word for it. With Desktop, you don’t have to. Download it, plug in your hardware, and see where it really works and where it doesn’t.


If something breaks,[open an issue](https://github.com/synnaxlabs/synnax/issues) and tell us.
